Did some more work on the headers protocol today. One of the things I wanted to look at was the benefit of obtaining identity hashes from the wire serialization (vs. the header.hash() method, which reserializes the header into the hash accumulator). The tradeoff is memory (caching the hashes) for speed (no need to reserialize to obtain the hash).

With headers the expected gain is minimal, since the reserialization is trivial. However, the net difference when applied to the headers message is about 35% reduction in header sync time. I found two very reliable peers, which have fast and reliable times for header sync. They average 14.5 seconds without the caching and 9.5 seconds with it.

This implies that the advantage to for applying this to tx hashing should be significant. Even 35% would be huge, but I'd guess we'd be closer to 50% improvement.

elements.text: Implemented basic blocks first sync yesterday. Spent today analyzing it. Overall everything is looking great. From a single peer I downloaded 480,555 blocks, parsed, hashed and stored all headers and txs. I stopped the run today to look at the flush behavior. It took about 15 minutes to flush that full run to my HDD (146.5GB). The network stop is always almost instant, only flushing the logging buffer will slow it down. The store stop is now isolated from that, so we get a clear measure and indication of store flush progress. I'm probably going to add events so that we can reflect progress. There are a lot of tables, and we can get feedback from the msync and fsync completion of each one. That's as good as it will get for the memory maps, but that's enough to know that it isn't dead. The event logging system can be used by a UI to provide progress/feedback for these types of things.

elements.text:
In the first run I encountered a simple script deserialization failure, which is resolved.

In the second run I encountered a link overflow. This was due to running multiple peers in a race for blocks. Since there is not yet a block chaser to eliminate redundancies, the store had a large amount of redundant writes (stopped at ~800GB at ~block 600,000). These become orphaned naturally and are not technically a problem. However the tables use byte-aligned internal links that are sized based on expected table size. This run overflowed the txs association table link (4 bytes), effectively killing the run. I hadn't added a runtime guard in for this scenario, but I figure it's worth the trivial extra check. So that's included now. The node will encounter a handled write failure in the case of link type overflow, and this implies that the node must be recompiled using a larger link capacity for that table. In v3 links were all either 32 or 64 bytes, which had the same issue but also wasted a huge amount of space. Presently we use 3/4/5 byte link sizes.

The third run (with one peer, so no redundancies) completed as expected. In analyzing sizes I noticed that the both this run and the previous overflowed the puts association table link. But in this case there would be no failure unless a read of the txs is attempted. In the case of txs there was a read in order to test for block existence, which caused the halt. The reason this run overflowed puts is that my estimate of inputs/outputs count was too low. As configured it was targeting 78% capacity, but it hit 104%. This means the link type for puts must be increased from 4 bytes to 5. That implies a .7GB store increase. All link types now have cushion in bitcoin for many years to come.

elements.text: Some observations regarding the memory map. My machine is 5 years old, has 256GB RAM, and a new 2TB SSD. As the run was completing I brought up the performance monitor and saw clearly that 255 GB of RAM was allocated to the process. There was a very consistent/flat level of reads that were roughly equal to the amount of writes, though the writes were very spikey. The reads are are expected to hit the hash table headers and walk hash deconfliction linked lists within the files, at arbitrary positions. Given that the store is close to twice my available RAM, this requires a material and very consistent level of memory map paging. This type of store is optimized for a machine with sufficient RAM available to hold the entire blockchain. That was the case when I bought this machine. My mac pro has 1TB RAM, which should make for some good stats. This store ideally targets NVRAM, eliminating paging altogether. But the interface is relational, allowing it to sit on a traditional SQL interface. As the sync completed I watched the SSD go to 100% and the RAM profile ramp down in opposition, until SSD went to 0% and RAM was at about 10%. This was the OS automatically unloading the pages that were no longer in use - as expected.

elements.text: Validation is partially ordered. Only the prevout tx for an input is required to validate the input. Once the set of inputs of a tx is validated, the tx is validated, and once the txs of a block are validated, the block is validated. While eventually all txs must be validated, making sequential validation (block order) the simplest approach, obtaining all txs in block order creates a significant ordering constraint on downloads. In that model the full sync can be no faster than the fastest peer's block transfer rate. But given multiple peers the theoretical limit to the transfer rate (setting aside marshalling cost) is the transfer time of just one block of max size. Given a concurrent peer limit, such as the max number of ports on a machine (2^16), this is currently the transfer time of 12 blocks of average size. So maximizing bandwidth is possible.

elements.text: At design time I was worried about
is_confirmable

due to the complexity of the relational query. Starting with a block height, the block fk is obtained, then all tx fks, then for each tx, all input fks, then for each input, a search for all spenders of the prevout of that input (by tx-hash/index hash table search key), then each spender is navigated to its tx, then its block fk, then the strong_bk table is searched for block confirmation. There are 2.16 billion inputs. So completing this query in 45 minutes across the entire blockchain is pretty amazing. And I'm glad I didn't try to optimize it with additional tables, since it doesn't appear limiting.

elements.text: Spent the day cleaning up sizing spreadsheets, updating table initialization defaults, reviewing capacity and perf. When some numbers didn't line up exactly I determined that I was incorrectly treating the validation tables as records but I had changed them to slabs so that values could be compressed. This creates a different link sizing requirement, and sure enough when I reviewed the link capacity, the
validated_tx
table was well over capacity. The
validated_bk
table was well below. This explained why
set_connected(tx)

population run accelerated significantly after a certain value. The link had overflowed, resulting in logical failures (which are fast). I'm summing up logical results, but there are expected failures due to the simulation. So after updating the build, the
set connected
run took 28 mins vs 9. All still constant time. This is still well within criteria, especially given that these calls will run concurrently.

elements.text: Looking at overall sizing, now that I have actual data vs. estimates. We have populated headers, bodies, and validation metadata. The only thing that isn't being populated at this point is query server optional data (address, neutrino) and two potential optimizing tables (bootstrap, buffer). So it's a good look at actual size for the current height. Total headers are 15.3GB at a collision rate of 1.5. This is what gets copied in a snapshot, and takes about 30 secs on my SSD. That can be cut in half by just doubling collision rate. I'll run some tests on idea collision rates at some point. Bodies are 518.6 GB, with some variability possible due to validation behavior. This can be trivially pruned to 501GB by deleting tx validation metadata once synced to a given height. 518 is still below the level projected by my original spreadsheet, at this height (525GB).

elements.text: Nothing too exciting today. Spent half the day chasing a bug. Was trivial thing, in tested database code, but the test was a little too simple. This was after doing multiple runs against a store to verify idempotency. So that's all good now. New code work was on incorporation of
chain_state

. This class is designed to init off the store and then prevent the need to ever hit the store (excepting chain splits) to determine chain state. The state just rolls forward in a simple struct from block to block. This was previous implementation that I adapted, almost the same. This hides all fork activation code and various ugly things like that, exposing it as a simple set of flags. Also maintains median time past, height and previous block hash. This can be set up to populate in full from the store for each block (how Core does it) or to roll state forward. I did the former yesterday and added the latter today. I measured the performance difference, and the roll forward cuts the typical full header sync time down from 30 secs to 15 secs. Without any validation or chain state the best I saw was 7-8 secs. With full header validation and rolling
chain_state

I saw a lot of 11-12 secs. This is obviously inconsequential for initial block download, but it does have bearing on the cost of validating a new block when the header arrives (mining scenario). The total time for one header, including network is about .015 ms.

elements.text: The aspect that this leaves out presently is the "chaser" object that manages and validates data fed from multiple concurrent peers into a single tree, determining the greatest work, and organizing that into the store. Presently it's just a single peer connection that validates and organizes into the store. The block download is also functional, but as was the case with headers, is not yet validating. Now that headers are storing their context (from chain state), blocks can be validated upon arrival. A couple days ago I did the work to size and verify the validation and confirmation metadata tables. So next step is to validate the full chain as it arrives from a single peer. I'll work on that next. Once that is done I'll implement
transaction_in

in a similar manner. Its chaser manages the tx pool. Then I'll add in the header/block/tx out protocols, which are even simpler than the incoming protocols. Then will move on to the chasers (header tree, concurrent block downloader/validator/confirmer, tx graph).
